record.paper_title: Open Problems in α Particle Condensation
record.original_question: How do three-fermion clusters such as nucleons or tritons dissolve into their constituents at higher density or temperature, and can neutron-rich α gases form resonant gases of n tritons described by an antisymmetrized trimer product wave function?

evidence.quote: For example nucleons are in first approximation strongly bound clusters of three quarks. Then at higher densities and/or temperatures it would be very interesting to know how these clusters dissolve into their constituents, or the other way round, a process known as hadronization.
A gas of nα particles where 2n neutrons are added may have a resonant state of n tritons. Formally such a gas of trimers again could be treated with a THSR wave function [56],
The antisymmetrizer will take care of the fact that the new gas of trimers builds up its proper Fermi surface.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a three-fermion cluster (e.g., a nucleon viewed as a bound state of three quarks, or a triton viewed as a bound state of two neutrons and one proton). Two related questions are posed:

(a) Dissolution of trimer clusters. Provide a quantitative theoretical description of how a system of three-fermion bound clusters dissolves into its constituent fermions as the density and/or temperature of the system is increased (the inverse process being a "hadronization"-type recombination). In particular, determine the critical line in the density–temperature plane at which the trimer bound states cease to exist as well-defined quasi-particles in the medium, and characterize the crossover from a gas of trimers to a degenerate Fermi gas of constituents.

(b) Trimer condensate ansatz. Consider a finite nucleus or nuclear gas consisting of n α-particles together with 2n additional neutrons, so that the system can be regarded as composed of n tritons (each triton being a bound state of two neutrons and one proton). Investigate whether such a system admits a resonant state describable by a Tohsaki–Horiuchi–Schuck–Röpke (THSR)–type product wave function of the form
   Ψ = 𝒜 { φ(R₁) φ(R₂) ⋯ φ(Rₙ) ⊗ χ(internal triton coordinates) },
where 𝒜 is the full antisymmetrizer over all constituent nucleons, Rᵢ denotes the center-of-mass coordinate of the i-th triton, φ is a common Gaussian (or analogous) single-trimer wave function describing condensation into a 0S center-of-mass orbital, and χ is the intrinsic triton wave function. The antisymmetrizer is required to enforce the proper Fermi surface of the trimer gas. Determine whether such a trimer-condensate state is energetically and dynamically realized (as a bound or resonant state) in neutron-rich nuclei or in low-density neutron-rich nuclear matter, and compute its properties.
artifact.status_search_result: Recent literature on the THSR wave function and α-particle condensation (e.g., reviews from 2016 onward and works on tetraneutron condensation in neutron-rich matter, 2019) continues to discuss trimer/cluster dissolution and neutron-rich cluster gases as ongoing research directions, without providing a definitive answer to the existence and properties of an antisymmetrized triton-product condensate or to the dissolution mechanism of three-fermion clusters at high density/temperature. The questions remain open.

status_evidence.title: Alpha particle clusters and their condensation in nuclear systems
status_evidence.snippet: Review discussing THSR wave function for α condensates and extensions to other cluster systems; trimer/triton condensates remain a speculative extension.
status_evidence.claim: The THSR framework for alpha condensation has been extended in various directions, but a triton-gas trimer condensate is discussed only as an open possibility.

status_evidence.title: Tetraneutron condensation in neutron rich matter
status_evidence.snippet: Investigates condensation of multi-neutron clusters in neutron-rich nuclear matter, indicating that cluster condensates in neutron-rich systems are still under active investigation.
status_evidence.claim: Cluster condensation phenomena in neutron-rich matter are an active and unresolved area of research.
